```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
# site builds: GADM files downloaded earlier, if STAREAL_GADM_CACHE names a folder of them
local({
  cache <- Sys.getenv("STAREAL_GADM_CACHE")
  if (nzchar(cache)) {
    dir.create(file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"), showWarnings = FALSE)
    file.copy(list.files(cache, pattern = "^gadm41_", full.names = TRUE), file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"))
  }
})
```

The fit of [tutorial 1](crt76t.html) had the default mean, an intercept and
a linear trend in time, and the spatial-temporal field did the rest.
Covariates move part of that variation into the mean. They can explain it,
and they let areas with the same covariate values borrow strength from each
other, including areas with no surveys.

*stareal* takes covariates as tables keyed by area, by time step, or by both.
This tutorial uses the crt K76T data of tutorial 1, and builds its
covariates from the frame itself: a smooth regional trend, and a contrast
between Kenya and Uganda and the rest of the region. The last section shows
how to build the same tables from a raster of your own, such as
transmission intensity or elevation.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. The data

As in tutorial 1, with the example data that ship with *stareal*:

```{r data, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
iso3 <- c("DJI", "ERI", "ETH", "KEN", "SOM", "SSD", "SDN", "UGA")
adm1 <- sf::st_as_sf(geodata::gadm(iso3, level = 1, path = tempdir(), version = "4.1", resolution = 2))
lakes <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 10, type = "lakes", category = "physical",
                                    returnclass = "sf", destdir = tempdir())
crs <- "+proj=laea +lat_0=8 +lon_0=37 +units=m"
adm1 <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(adm1, crs))
lakes <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(lakes, crs))
lakes <- lakes[as.numeric(sf::st_area(lakes)) > 1e9, ]
water <- sf::st_intersection(sf::st_union(lakes), sf::st_union(adm1))
adm1 <- sf::st_difference(adm1, water)
adm1 <- adm1[adm1$ENGTYPE_1 != "Water body", ]           # what is left of Uganda's lake units
fr <- areal_frame(adm1, id = "GID_1", groups = c(country = "COUNTRY"), link_within = "country",
                  verbose = FALSE)
tf <- time_frame(1989, 2024, "month")
d <- areal_data(igad_crt76t, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day", verbose = FALSE)
```

## 2. Three kinds of covariate table

A covariate table is an ordinary data frame. Its key columns say what it
varies over:

| Key columns | Varies by | One row per |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | area | area |
| `time` (labels) or `t` (step numbers) | time step | time step |
| `id` and `time` (or `t`) | area and time step | area-time cell |

Every other column is a covariate, named in the formula as it is named in
the table. **A table must cover every area, every step or every cell of the
frame**, not just the surveyed ones, because `predict()` needs the
covariates everywhere. Transforms and interactions are computed as columns
first: the formula takes plain names (and `trend()`), not `log(x)` or
`x:z`.

The three tables of this tutorial:

```{r tables}
# by time: a natural spline in calendar time, 3 degrees of freedom
year <- 1989 + (seq_len(tf$n_steps) - 1) / 12
basis <- splines::ns(year, df = 3)
by_time <- data.frame(time = tf$labels, s1 = basis[, 1], s2 = basis[, 2], s3 = basis[, 3])

# by area: 1 in Kenya and Uganda, 0 elsewhere
by_area <- data.frame(id = fr$ids, ku = as.numeric(fr$groups$country %in% c("Kenya", "Uganda")))

# by area and time: ku times a linear trend from -1 in the first month to 1 in the last
by_cell <- expand.grid(id = fr$ids, time = tf$labels, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
by_cell$ku_trend <- by_area$ku[match(by_cell$id, by_area$id)] *
  seq(-1, 1, length.out = tf$n_steps)[match(by_cell$time, tf$labels)]

head(by_time, 3)
head(by_area, 3)
c(rows = nrow(by_cell), areas = fr$m, steps = tf$n_steps)
```

`ku_trend` is built to match `trend()`, which also runs from −1 at the
first step to 1 at the last.

### Standardised or not

By default, numeric covariates are standardised: mean 0 and sd 1 over the
areas, steps or cells of their table. A coefficient is then the effect of
one sd, and the default prior on the fixed effects (normal, sd 3 on the
logit scale) suits any units. Factors become one 0/1 column per level after
the first, and are not standardised.

The covariates here are already on a unit scale, and their coefficients are
easier to read unstandardised, so the fits below use
`scale_covariates = FALSE`. With covariates in large units, such as
population or rainfall in millimetres, keep the default.

## 3. A covariate by time: a smooth regional trend

`trend()` makes the regional mean a straight line on the logit scale.
Anything else, such as a decline that starts late and then levels off, is
left to the field. A spline basis in the year lets the mean bend:

```{r fit-smooth, message = FALSE}
fit_smooth <- fit_areal(d, ~ s1 + s2 + s3, covariates = by_time, scale_covariates = FALSE)
diagnose(fit_smooth)$checks
summary(fit_smooth)
```

For comparison, the fit of tutorial 1, with the default `~ trend()`:

```{r fit-linear, message = FALSE}
fit_linear <- fit_areal(d)
```

The spline coefficients mean little one by one. The curve they make does:
the regional mean on the prevalence scale, draw by draw, beside the
straight line of tutorial 1. (This is the prevalence where the field is
zero, roughly the median unit, not the average over units.)

```{r smooth-curve, fig.height = 4}
curve <- function(fit, X) {
  b <- posterior::as_draws_matrix(fit)[, colnames(X)]
  p <- plogis(unclass(b) %*% t(X))
  data.frame(year = year, mean = colMeans(p),
             lo = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.025), hi = apply(p, 2, quantile, 0.975))
}
X_smooth <- cbind(intercept = 1, by_time[, c("s1", "s2", "s3")])
X_linear <- cbind(intercept = 1, trend = seq(-1, 1, length.out = tf$n_steps))
both <- rbind(cbind(curve(fit_smooth, as.matrix(X_smooth)), mean_model = "spline (this tutorial)"),
              cbind(curve(fit_linear, X_linear), mean_model = "linear trend (tutorial 1)"))
ggplot(both, aes(year, mean, colour = mean_model, fill = mean_model)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "K76T prevalence, regional mean", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r hyper, include = FALSE}
hyper <- function(fit, v) summary(fit)$table[summary(fit)$table$variable == v, ]
```

The straight line cannot bend. The spline shows the shape the data
support: K76T close to fixation from the late 1990s to about 2008, then a
fall, steepest after 2010. Two things qualify it:

- **The bands are wide.** The curve is the prevalence where the field is
  zero. With `rho_s` and `rho_t` both close to 1, the field has a slowly
  varying region-wide component of its own, and it trades off against the
  fixed effects. The data fix their sum better than either part.
- **A regional curve averages unlike places.** Since 2015 there have been
  65 surveys in Kenya and Uganda, where K76T fell, and 57 elsewhere,
  mostly in Ethiopia and Sudan, where it is still common. The fall after
  2015 is an average of the two, and true of neither. Section 4 separates
  them. The rise before 1995 rests on only 6 surveys, and may not be real.

The hyperparameters change too. `rho_s` falls from
`r round(hyper(fit_linear, "rho_s")$mean, 2)` with the straight line to
`r round(hyper(fit_smooth, "rho_s")$mean, 2)` with the spline, and its
interval widens. The reason is in the Leroux prior: the variance of the
field's average over the whole region is proportional to
`sigma^2 / (1 - rho_s)`. With a straight-line mean, the field has to carry
the bend in the regional curve, and a `rho_s` close to 1 is what lets it.
With the bend in the mean, it needs less of that. A covariate changes what
the field has to explain, so the field's parameters are only comparable
between models with the same mean.

## 4. Covariates by area, and by area and time

The country curves of tutorial 1 suggest that K76T fell sooner in Kenya and
Uganda than elsewhere. Is the difference real, or could the field have made
it by chance? `ku` shifts the level in Kenya and Uganda, measured at the
middle of the window, where `trend()` is 0. `ku_trend` changes their slope:

Several tables go in as a list. Each covariate must be in exactly one of
them.

```{r fit-ku, message = FALSE}
fit_ku <- fit_areal(d, ~ trend() + ku + ku_trend, covariates = list(by_area, by_cell),
                    scale_covariates = FALSE)
diagnose(fit_ku)$checks
summary(fit_ku)
```

The posterior probability that the decline was steeper in Kenya and Uganda
is the share of draws with `ku_trend` below zero:

```{r ku-prob}
b <- posterior::as_draws_matrix(fit_ku)
mean(b[, "ku_trend"] < 0)
```

The probability is close to 1: the decline was steeper in Kenya and
Uganda, and the field, which could have produced a local decline on its
own, does not account for the difference. Read the coefficients together:

- `trend` is now the slope outside Kenya and Uganda, and it is close to
  zero (`r round(hyper(fit_ku, "trend")$mean, 1)`, with an interval from
  `r round(hyper(fit_ku, "trend")$q2.5, 1)` to
  `r round(hyper(fit_ku, "trend")$q97.5, 1)`). Ethiopia's and Sudan's
  recent surveys still find K76T in most infections.
- `trend + ku_trend` is the slope in Kenya and Uganda, about
  `r round(hyper(fit_ku, "trend")$mean + hyper(fit_ku, "ku_trend")$mean, 1)`:
  a fall of about
  `r round(-2 * (hyper(fit_ku, "trend")$mean + hyper(fit_ku, "ku_trend")$mean))`
  on the logit scale over the window.
- `ku`, the difference in level at the middle of the window (late 2006),
  has an interval that spans zero.

`sigma` falls, from `r round(hyper(fit_linear, "sigma")$mean, 1)` to
`r round(hyper(fit_ku, "sigma")$mean, 1)`, as the contrast takes over part
of the variation that the field carried.

## 5. A factor level with no data

Is K76T different in cities? GADM gives Ethiopia's two chartered cities,
Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa, units of their own. Neither has a crt survey, so
the data say nothing about a city effect. `fit_areal()` says so before it
starts sampling:

```{r uninformed}
by_type <- data.frame(id = fr$ids,
                      setting = factor(ifelse(adm1$ENGTYPE_1[match(fr$ids, adm1$GID_1)] == "City", "city", "other"),
                                       levels = c("other", "city")))
tryCatch(fit_areal(d, ~ trend() + setting, covariates = by_type, control = list(verbose = FALSE)),
         warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
```

The posterior of `settingcity` would be its prior, and every prediction for
the two cities would carry that prior's uncertainty, on top of the field's.
Three remedies:

- **Merge the level** with others, as `ku` does for the countries outside
  Kenya and Uganda.
- **Give it an informative prior**, by name:
  `priors = areal_priors(beta_sd = c(settingcity = 0.5))`.
- **Leave the covariate out** and let the field carry the differences, as
  in tutorial 1.

A factor's first level is its baseline, and the levels are alphabetical by
default. Above, `levels = c("other", "city")` makes the surveyed units the
baseline; alphabetical order would have made the unsurveyed cities the
baseline instead.

## 6. Predicting with covariates

Nothing changes: `predict()` evaluates the covariates in every area and
month from the tables the fit was given.

```{r predict}
pr_ku <- predict(fit_ku, groups = "country", verbose = FALSE)
pr_linear <- predict(fit_linear, groups = "country", verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r predict-compare, fig.height = 4.5}
countries <- c("Kenya", "Uganda", "Ethiopia", "Sudan")
cmp <- rbind(cbind(pr_linear$groups$country, model = "~ trend() (tutorial 1)"),
             cbind(pr_ku$groups$country, model = "~ trend() + ku + ku_trend"))
cmp <- cmp[cmp$id %in% countries, ]
ggplot(cmp, aes(date, mean, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~id) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "K76T prevalence", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r compare-2024, include = FALSE}
at <- function(pr, country) {
  g <- pr$groups$country
  g$mean[g$id == country & g$time == "2024-07"]
}
```

In Kenya and Uganda the two models agree: the data there decide. In
Ethiopia and Sudan they part after the last surveys (2022 in Ethiopia,
2018 in Sudan). Tutorial 1's model carries the region's decline into them.
The covariate model does not, because the decline belongs to Kenya and
Uganda. In July 2024 it puts Ethiopia at about
`r round(100 * at(pr_ku, "Ethiopia"))`%, against
`r round(100 * at(pr_linear, "Ethiopia"))`%, and Sudan at about
`r round(100 * at(pr_ku, "Sudan"))`%, against
`r round(100 * at(pr_linear, "Sudan"))`%. Neither number comes from recent
data in those countries. Each follows from what the mean assumes where the
surveys stop. A covariate changes the map most where the data are
thinnest, which is where it most needs to be right.

Whether either covariate model predicts better than tutorial 1's is a
question for [cross-validation](crossval.html), which compares them with
it, and with two simpler models, on the same held-out surveys.

## 7. Your own covariates from a raster

Most real covariates come as rasters: transmission intensity, rainfall,
elevation, population. `exactextractr` averages a raster over each
polygon, and a raster with one layer per time step gives a table by area
and time step:

```{r raster, eval = FALSE}
r <- terra::rast("my_covariate.tif")             # one layer per month, named "2000-01", "2000-02", ...
ex <- exactextractr::exact_extract(r, adm1, "mean")
by_cell <- data.frame(id = rep(adm1$GID_1, times = ncol(ex)),
                      time = rep(sub("^mean[.]", "", names(ex)), each = nrow(ex)),
                      my_covariate = unlist(ex, use.names = FALSE))
```

A yearly raster with a monthly time frame gives each month its year's
value: match on the year of each time label.

Two things to settle before fitting:

- **Coverage.** The table must cover every time step of the time frame. A
  raster that starts later than the surveys needs a stated rule for the
  earlier steps, such as holding the first value, or a shorter time frame.
- **Area, not survey.** A covariate here describes an area in a time step,
  and must be known for every one of them. Properties of a survey (the study
  design, the sampled population) are not covariates of this model.
